prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I hold B008 as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye. The round-1 record has sharpened the case rather than weakened it. Six of eight members prefer it and the two who do not (Eriksson, Mehlig) name it as their first alternative, but I treat that only as a signal that the arguments were tested from different subfields. The substance is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new architecture: it cancels Doppler, recoil and lattice Stark shifts while interrogating many neutral atoms in parallel, which is what moved optical clocks from the 1e-16 regime to about 1e-18. The performance is reproduced in Sr, Yb and Hg at several national laboratories, with routine comparisons, and it feeds relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and the planned SI second. Lindroth's atomic-structure assessment of the magic-wavelength condition and the systematic budget, which I cannot make from my own field, removes my main worry about robustness of the 1e-18 claims. The attribution is a two-name pair that follows concept plus first realisation (Katori) and record accuracy plus many-body operation (Ye). On the chair's question about citation wording, I propose 'for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock', which names the lattice concept itself, does not mention optical clocks or timekeeping generally, and does not mention the redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains distinctness from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser background sits close to the 2005 work. I now think it is answerable: the comb supplies the counting mechanism and Wineland the control of single quantum systems, whereas a neutral-atom lattice at a magic wavelength is neither, so the citation should say lattice clock and no more. What is not answered is credit outside the two names. NIST, PTB, SYRTE, Tokyo and the Yb and Hg groups, and the early lattice-clock proposals, hold claims that a two-name prize cannot reflect, and I rely on recalled history for priority rather than on verified sources. I also take Eriksson's point that the clock is a large gain in precision more than a change in how we understand matter. I weigh the tests of relativity and constants as physics, but I accept that this is a judgment on which a member can reasonably differ. The pending SI redefinition cuts either way and I do not let it carry weight.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a quantitative prediction followed by a decisive experiment, and calls the clock a large precision gain without a comparable change in how we understand matter.
responses.response: I accept that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is a striking pairing, and I agree with you that a prize may precede a mechanism. My difficulty is the credit set, not the physics: you concede that Cao and the parallel experimental groups sit outside the three names, and Olsson argues that this gap is not minor. On weight, I think the clock is more than precision. It makes relativistic time dilation measurable across a millimetre-scale sample and gives laboratory sensitivity to drifts of constants, which is physics and not only metrology. I still rank B035 seventh, and I would want the mechanism debate and the credit question to settle further before a three-name split. It would not move me to give it priority this year.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers trapped-ion quantum logic (Cirac, Zoller, Blatt) as a thirty-year, widely confirmed line, concedes that the experimental share is contestable, and says the overlap argument against the clock also applies to B008.
responses.response: I accept your point that overlap with earlier prizes is a symmetric argument and I have tried to meet it on B008 directly rather than ignore it. On B022 I still think the weak point is the experimental share: the first entangling gates came substantially from NIST and Innsbruck, and Wineland's 2012 recognition covered the underlying ion control. Naming Blatt is a judgment call, as you say. That leaves B008 as the pair with a cleaner chain from invention to demonstration. I do not rule out B022 for a later year, and I keep it as my second alternative, but I would need a principled basis for the third name before I support it ahead of the clock.

responses.point: Olsson prefers aberration-corrected microscopy first on opening but now holds B008 as her stated preference, and presses that the committee should say the prize is for the invention and not for the whole field of optical clocks.
responses.response: I agree with that framing and would hold the citation to the lattice clock itself. We should say in committee discussion that the prize is not a complete allocation of the optical-clock field, since PTB, SYRTE, NIST and others have real claims. On B009 I still regard the achievement as mature and overdue, but I keep it as a first alternative and not a co-part: Krivanek's independent STEM correction work cannot be covered by Rose, Haider and Urban, and the payoff lies mainly in materials and chemistry. I also note your recusal caution on B009 and would treat it as a reason to discount your view there only if the committee reaches that candidate.

responses.point: Danielsson says the novelty objection is not fully answered by 'already honoured or separable' and that the citation must explain why the lattice is a distinct invention, and he would prefer a Higgs part over IceCube if a second part is wanted.
responses.response: I agree with the first point and propose the narrow wording above. On a second part, I do not support B056 because the three-name limit forces an arbitrary choice from Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and Olsson's different subset shows this is not a small matter. As an experimentalist from large collaborations I would not want a prize to rest on a spokesperson convention. On IceCube I accept your view that the diffuse flux is the larger event and the source identifications are still maturing, and I have moved it out of my alternatives for this cycle.

responses.point: Kroll reports finding no second part stronger than the clock alone, and says the redefinition of the SI second is not a reason to hurry or delay.
responses.response: I agree and I have looked for a second part that adds to the clock and have not found one with a settled credit set. B009 has the Krivanek problem, B022 has the Blatt allocation, B035 has maturity and the Cao gap, and B049 omits Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan, as Lindroth notes. A weak second part would dilute a clean single award, so I propose B008 alone. I also record your disclosed link to Hall's laboratory; it does not change my reading of the evidence.

uncertainties: Priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and the first Sr lattice-clock demonstrations, and the weight of NIST, PTB, SYRTE and Yb or Hg groups; I rely on recalled history and not on verified sources.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes on the strength of a narrowly worded citation.
Whether a member who judges the clock mainly as precision would hold that it falls short of the weight the committee wants for a physics prize.
Whether a single-part prize is preferable to a two-part prize if a candidate with a settled credit set emerged.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B008 from my profile: my documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH) concern astroparticle detectors. I remain in the field of B042 IceCube, which I no longer list as an alternative, and I would step aside from any decision on it if the committee reached it. As chair I have tried to state the counter-arguments to B008 at full strength.
